GOV-01.title: Code of Conduct & Ethics
GOV-01.description: {company_name} maintains a Code of Conduct that sets expected standards of behavior for everyone working on its behalf, including contractors. Personnel acknowledge it, and deviations are addressed through documented procedures.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization have a Code of Conduct or ethics document that employees are expected to follow? (Yes/No)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have code of conduct and ethics practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.
collection.question: Does your company have a Code of Conduct that all employees and contractors must acknowledge?
follow_ups: How often do employees re-acknowledge it (annually, at onboarding only)?
Does it cover contractors and third-party personnel?
What happens when someone violates the Code of Conduct?

evidence_goals: Pull the current Code of Conduct document showing the standards of behavior it defines and a visible approval or effective date
Pull the documented disciplinary or violation handling procedure that applies when the Code is breached
Pull acknowledgment records for a sample of personnel, including contractors, showing each person accepted the current version within the required period
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: The approved Code document with a visible effective or approval date, the written disciplinary procedure, and per person acknowledgment records from the HR or onboarding system showing names and dates that fall within the required re-acknowledgment window and cover contractors as well as employees.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: A statement that a Code exists without the document itself, the document with no acknowledgment records, or acknowledgments that predate the current version of the Code.
red_flags: Code has no approval or effective date, or is visibly outdated
Contractors and third party personnel are excluded from acknowledgment
Acknowledgment happens only at first hire with no periodic re-acknowledgment
No written disciplinary process for violations
Acknowledgment records cover only a fraction of active personnel

platform_hints.google_workspace: The Code often lives in Drive with acknowledgments collected through a Google Form; pull the response sheet showing names and dates.
platform_hints.rippling: Pull the onboarding acknowledgment task or policy sign off report showing per person completion, including any contractor records.
platform_hints.gusto: Pull the document acknowledgment or signature report from the onboarding checklist showing who signed and when.
platform_hints.notion: The Code may be a Notion page; the acknowledgment evidence still needs to come from a signature tool or HR record, not the page view history.

GOV-02.title: Governance Oversight
GOV-02.description: Oversight of the security and internal control program rests with {governance_body}. Control effectiveness and management's performance are evaluated periodically, and meetings and decisions are documented.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization have a governance body (such as a board of directors, advisory board, security committee, or leadership team) that meets to discuss security or risk topics? (Yes/No, informal arrangements count as yes)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have governance oversight practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.
collection.question: Who provides oversight of your security and internal controls program, and how often do they meet?
follow_ups: Is this a board, advisory board, leadership team, or single person?
How often do they review security matters (quarterly, annually)?
Are meeting discussions and decisions documented?
Does anyone on this body have security or compliance expertise?

evidence_goals: Pull documentation identifying the governance body and its defined oversight responsibilities for security and internal controls
Pull a roster or bios showing member expertise and at least one member independent from day to day management
Pull minutes or notes from a sample of meetings showing security topics on the agenda and decisions or action items recorded and tracked to closure
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: A charter or terms of reference naming the governance body and its security oversight duties, a roster showing member backgrounds and at least one member independent of daily operations, plus dated meeting minutes where a security topic appears and action items are assigned and later followed up.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: A claim that leadership discusses security with no minutes, minutes with no security content, or a body with no identified expertise or independence from management.
red_flags: No written minutes or notes for any meeting
Security never appears on any agenda across the sampled meetings
Action items are recorded but never tracked to closure
Every member is part of daily management with no independent voice
The body exists on paper but has not met within the last 12 months

platform_hints.notion: Agendas and minutes are commonly kept as dated Notion pages; pull the pages showing security topics and tracked action items.
platform_hints.google_workspace: Recurring meeting cadence shows in Calendar and minutes in Docs; pull both to evidence frequency and content.

GOV-03.title: Organizational Structure & Responsibilities
GOV-03.description: {company_name} maintains an organizational structure with defined reporting lines, authorities, and responsibilities across the organization.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization have a defined structure with reporting lines and assigned security responsibilities? (Yes/No, even if informal)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have organizational structure and responsibilities practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.
collection.question: Can you describe your organizational structure and how security responsibilities are assigned?
follow_ups: Do you have an org chart with reporting lines?
Who is ultimately responsible for security (CISO, CTO, CEO)?
How is separation of duties handled?
Are security authorities and responsibilities documented?

evidence_goals: Pull the current organizational chart showing reporting lines across the organization
Pull documentation assigning security, compliance, and privacy responsibilities to named roles, including a designated privacy owner
Pull evidence that critical functions are separated between different people, or where headcount prevents this, the documented compensating controls such as review or approval workflows
Pull documentation assigning ownership of key external relationships
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: A dated org chart with clear reporting lines plus a responsibility document or matrix naming who owns security, compliance, privacy, and key vendor relationships, and where separation of duties is not feasible a written description of the compensating review or approval controls.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: A verbal description of who does what with no chart or written assignment, or an org chart with no security or privacy ownership defined anywhere.
red_flags: No designated privacy owner
Security responsibility is assumed but never assigned in writing
One person holds conflicting duties with no documented compensating control
Org chart is undated or clearly stale
Key external relationships have no assigned owner

platform_hints.rippling: Pull the org chart generated from the HRIS showing reporting lines and titles.
platform_hints.gusto: Pull the company org chart and role assignments from the HR directory.
platform_hints.notion: Responsibility matrices and role ownership docs often live in Notion; pull the page defining security, compliance, and privacy owners.

GOV-04.title: Leadership & Advisor Oversight of Security
GOV-04.description: {company_name} reports security and compliance status to leadership, advisors, or investors on a recurring cadence, keeping someone independent of day-to-day engineering informed of the security program.

collection.gating_question: Does someone outside your day-to-day engineering work, such as a founder, an advisor, or your investors, receive updates on your security and compliance status on a regular basis? (Yes/No, informal updates count as yes)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have leadership and advisor oversight of security practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.
collection.question: Who outside of day-to-day engineering is kept informed about your security and compliance status, and how often?
follow_ups: Is this a founder, a chief executive, an external advisor, an advisory board, or your investors?
How often do they receive security or compliance updates (monthly, quarterly, alongside investor updates)?
Do those updates include real status such as open risks, incidents, or compliance progress?
Are the updates written down or otherwise recorded?

PPL-01.title: Background Checks
PPL-01.description: {company_name} performs background checks on all new personnel including contractors prior to or upon their start date, including at minimum criminal history and employment verification.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization perform background checks on new employees or contractors? (Yes/No)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have background checks practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.
collection.question: Do you perform background checks on new employees and contractors before or when they start?
follow_ups: What does the check include (criminal history, employment verification)?
Does it cover contractors and temporary workers?
Are checks completed before the start date or within a grace period?

evidence_goals: Pull the written policy requiring background checks for all personnel including contractors prior to or upon start date, and defining the minimum check scope
Pull completed background check records from the screening vendor for a sample of recent hires showing the check was run and its scope
Pull hire records tying each sampled check to its subject and start date so timing against policy can be assessed
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: The screening policy stating who is covered, the timing requirement, and the minimum scope such as criminal history and employment verification, plus results or completion confirmations from the screening vendor for a sample of hires dated on or before each person's start date.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: A policy with no completed check records, a vendor invoice with no per person results, or checks whose scope cannot be confirmed against the policy minimum.
red_flags: Contractors or temporary workers are excluded from screening
Checks completed well after the start date with no documented interim control
Scope of the check cannot be confirmed to meet the policy minimum
Screening relies on candidate self attestation rather than an independent check
No records for a portion of sampled hires

platform_hints.checkr: Pull the per candidate report or completed status showing the check package and date; the package name should map to the policy minimum scope.
platform_hints.rippling: Pull the onboarding record showing screening status and completion date per new hire, including contractors.
platform_hints.deel: Contractor onboarding records show whether screening was required and completed for non employee personnel.

PPL-02.title: Job Descriptions & Competency
PPL-02.description: {company_name} maintains job descriptions defining required competencies and qualifications for key roles. Competence is evaluated and shortcomings are addressed.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization have written job descriptions or role definitions? (Yes/No)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have job descriptions and competency practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.
collection.question: Do you maintain formal job descriptions for key roles, especially those with security responsibilities?
follow_ups: Do descriptions include security-related competencies?
How is competence evaluated during hiring and ongoing?

evidence_goals: Pull job descriptions for key roles showing defined responsibilities and required competencies or qualifications
Pull documentation of the process used to evaluate competency at hiring and on an ongoing basis and to address shortcomings
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: Written job descriptions for key and security relevant roles that list required skills and qualifications, plus a described or evidenced process such as interview scorecards or periodic competency reviews showing how competence is assessed and gaps are closed.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: Generic recruiting posts with no competency requirements, or job descriptions with no accompanying evaluation process to assess or develop competence.
red_flags: Job descriptions omit any security or control competencies for relevant roles
No process to evaluate competence beyond the initial interview
Identified shortcomings are never addressed
Descriptions exist for only some key roles

platform_hints.rippling: Pull role definitions or stored job descriptions attached to positions in the HRIS.
platform_hints.notion: Job descriptions and competency matrices are often kept as Notion pages; pull the pages for key roles.
platform_hints.ashby: Interview scorecards and structured evaluations in the applicant tracking system evidence how competence is assessed at hiring.

PPL-03.title: Training & Competency Development
PPL-03.description: {company_name} requires all personnel to complete security awareness training periodically and upon onboarding for new personnel, covering relevant security topics. Personnel in security-relevant roles receive role-specific technical training.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization provide security awareness training to employees? (Yes/No, even annual or onboarding-only)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have training and competency development practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.
collection.question: Do you require security awareness training for all employees?
follow_ups: How often is training required (annually, at onboarding)?
What topics does it cover?
Do people in security-relevant roles get additional specialized training?

evidence_goals: Pull the security awareness training curriculum or course content showing the topics covered
Pull the training policy defining timing for new personnel and ongoing completion requirements, plus any role specific technical training requirements
Pull completion records for a sample of personnel showing training was completed within the required period
Pull evidence of role specific training or continuing education for a sample of security role personnel
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: The training content or platform course outline, a policy stating when training is due, and per person completion records exported from the training platform showing names and completion dates inside the required window, plus certificates or course records for specialized roles.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: A statement that training happens with no course content or completion records, completion figures with no per person dates, or a client authored spreadsheet asserting everyone was trained.
red_flags: Completion records missing for a meaningful share of active personnel
Training completion dates fall outside the required period
No onboarding training requirement for new hires
Role specific technical training is required on paper but never evidenced
Completion is tracked only in a client authored spreadsheet with no platform export behind it

platform_hints.knowbe4: Pull the training campaign completion report showing per user status and completion date.
platform_hints.google_workspace: A Forms based quiz with a linked response Sheet can evidence completion, but it must show per person names and dates.
platform_hints.rippling: If training runs through the built in learning module, pull the course completion report per employee.

PPL-04.title: Performance & Accountability
PPL-04.description: Security and internal control responsibilities are included in performance evaluation criteria, and corrective action is taken when they are not met. Excessive workload pressures are evaluated and adjusted.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization have a formal performance evaluation or accountability process? (Yes/No)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have performance and accountability practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.
collection.question: Are security responsibilities part of employee performance evaluations?
follow_ups: How are security responsibilities measured?
What happens when someone doesn't meet their security obligations?
How do you identify and address excessive pressures on employees?

evidence_goals: Pull the performance evaluation template or criteria showing security and control responsibilities are part of the assessment
Pull documentation defining consequences for policy violations including privacy violations
Pull completed performance evaluations for a sample of personnel dated within the required period
Where violations occurred, pull records showing corrective action was taken and documented
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: An evaluation template that explicitly references security or control duties, a written consequence or disciplinary schedule, and completed dated reviews for a sample of staff, plus corrective action records for any violations that arose during the period.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: A review template with no security content, a claim that reviews happen with no completed examples, or violations handled verbally with no record of corrective action.
red_flags: Security responsibilities are absent from the evaluation criteria
No completed reviews for sampled personnel within the period
Consequences for violations including privacy violations are undefined
Violations occurred but no corrective action was documented
Reviews exist but excessive workload pressures on personnel are never assessed

platform_hints.lattice: Pull the review cycle report showing completion status and dates, and the template showing security or control criteria.
platform_hints.15five: Pull the completed review records and the question set evidencing security responsibilities are assessed.
platform_hints.rippling: Performance review cycles and disciplinary records both live in the HRIS; pull completion status and any documented corrective actions.

PPL-05.title: Key Personnel & Continuity
PPL-05.description: {company_name} identifies key personnel dependencies for critical functions. Cross-training, documented procedures, or succession planning ensures continuity if key individuals become unavailable.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization have a plan or process for key personnel continuity (if a critical person leaves)? (Yes/No)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have key personnel and continuity practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.
collection.question: Do you have plans for continuity if key personnel become unavailable?
follow_ups: Have you identified which roles are key person dependencies?
Is there cross-training or documented procedures for critical functions?

evidence_goals: Pull documentation identifying key personnel and the critical functions that depend on them
Pull the documented continuity measures such as cross training records, runbooks, or succession plans that keep those functions running if an individual becomes unavailable
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: A written identification of key person dependencies for critical functions plus concrete continuity measures such as documented runbooks, named backups, or cross training records tied to each dependency.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: A general statement that the team could cover for each other, or a list of key people with no continuity measures attached to them.
red_flags: Key person dependencies are not identified
Continuity is asserted verbally with no runbooks or named backups
A single individual holds sole knowledge of a critical function
Documented procedures exist but are clearly stale

platform_hints.notion: Runbooks, succession notes, and key person mappings are commonly kept as Notion pages; pull the pages tied to critical functions.
platform_hints.github: Operational runbooks often live as markdown in a repository; pull the documented procedures for critical functions.
platform_hints.google_workspace: Continuity or succession plans stored in Drive; pull the current versions.

PPL-06.title: Contractor & Outsourced Personnel Controls
PPL-06.description: {company_name} holds contractors and outsourced personnel who can reach production systems or customer data to the same personnel and access controls as employees, from signed confidentiality agreements before access through standard offboarding and periodic access reviews.

collection.gating_question: Do any contractors or outsourced personnel have access to your production systems or customer data? (Yes/No)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have contractor and outsourced personnel controls in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.
collection.question: For any contractors or outsourced personnel who can access production systems or customer data, how are they vetted, given access, and removed?
follow_ups: Do contractors sign a confidentiality or security agreement before they get access?
Is their access created and removed through the same onboarding and offboarding process used for employees?
Are contractor accounts included when you run your periodic access reviews?
Where do contractors get access (code repositories, cloud console, customer database, internal tools)?
documents: Identity Provider (Okta / Azure AD / Google Workspace)

evidence_commands.shows: Lists external collaborators, which for most teams are contractors, who have access to the GitHub organization. Confirm every name is an expected current contractor and that departed contractors do not appear.

Lists Google Workspace accounts in the contractor org unit with suspended status, creation time, and last login. Confirm active accounts map to current contractors and that ended engagements show suspended as True.

Lists 1Password members of type guest, which are external contractors, with their state. Confirm each guest is a current contractor with a legitimate need for shared vault access and that former contractors are not still active.

evidence_goals: Obtain the list of contractors and outsourced personnel who have or had production or customer data access during the period
Show that each such contractor was under a signed confidentiality and security agreement dated before access was granted
Show that contractor access was created through the standard onboarding process and removed when the engagement ended
Show that contractor accounts are included in the periodic user access review population
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: A contractor roster that reconciles to the identity provider and repository access lists, signed agreements dated before access was granted, onboarding and offboarding tickets for each contractor, and a user access review that lists contractor accounts alongside employees.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: A verbal claim that contractors sign agreements with no signed documents produced, contractor accounts that appear in the identity provider or code repository but on no roster, or departed contractors that still show active access.
red_flags: Outside collaborators or guest accounts that map to no known current contractor
Departed contractors with active accounts or repository access
Contractors excluded from the user access review population
Access granted before any agreement was signed

platform_hints.github: Pull outside collaborators for the organization and their repository permissions. Reconcile against the contractor roster and check for departed contractors still listed.
platform_hints.google_workspace: Pull the contractor org unit user list with suspended status, creation time, and last login. Suspended accounts should correspond to ended engagements.
platform_hints.1password: Pull the member list and filter for guest accounts. Guests are external collaborators with limited vault access; confirm each is a current contractor.
platform_hints.okta: Pull users filtered to the contractor group with status and last login. Deactivated users should correspond to ended engagements.

POL-01.title: Policy Suite & Governance
POL-01.description: {company_name} maintains a formally approved policy suite covering the required security domains, from access control through business continuity. Each policy has a named owner, is reviewed periodically, and is put into action through operational procedures.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization have written security policies or procedures? (Yes/No, even if they need updating)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have policy suite and governance practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.
collection.question: Do you have a formal set of security policies covering access control, change management, incident response, data protection, and other key areas?
follow_ups: Which specific policies do you have?
Who owns each policy and how often are they reviewed?
Do you have operational procedures that put these policies into action?
Are security and compliance objectives formally defined?

evidence_goals: Pull the full set of approved policies covering access control, change management, incident response, data protection, acceptable use, vendor management, risk management, and business continuity
Pull evidence that each policy has an assigned owner and an approval and review date meeting the required review frequency
Pull the operational procedures that put the policies into action
Pull the documented security and compliance objectives and the process for communicating policies to personnel
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: The complete policy suite with each document showing an owner, an approval signature or record, and a review date within the required frequency, backed by operational procedures and a stated set of security and compliance objectives aligned with the entity's commitments.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: A single combined document that gestures at several areas, policies with no owner or approval date, or clearly templated policies with no procedures and no evidence of review.
red_flags: One or more required policy areas is missing
Policies have no assigned owner
Approval or last review date is missing or older than the required review frequency
Policies are clearly templated with no tailoring to the actual environment
No operational procedures exist to implement the policies
Security and compliance objectives are undefined

platform_hints.notion: A policy repository in Notion can show each policy with an owner property and last reviewed date; pull the database view plus the individual policy pages.
platform_hints.github: Policies kept as versioned markdown show approval and review history through commit and pull request records; pull the files and their history.
platform_hints.google_workspace: Policies in Drive should carry visible owner and approval or review dates; pull the documents and any approval records rather than a folder listing.

POL-02.title: Policy Communication & Accessibility
POL-02.description: Security policies, objectives, and responsibilities are kept somewhere accessible, and changes are communicated to affected personnel. Incident reporting channels and system boundaries are documented and shared with authorized users.

collection.gating_question: Are your security policies communicated to employees and accessible to them? (Yes/No)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have policy communication and accessibility practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.
collection.question: How do you communicate security policies and updates to your team?
follow_ups: Where are policies stored so employees can access them?
How are policy changes communicated?
How can employees report security incidents or concerns?

evidence_goals: Pull the configuration of where policies are stored and how they are made accessible (intranet, wiki, document management system)
Pull access permissions showing all relevant personnel can reach the policy repository
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: Config showing policy repository location (Notion, Confluence, SharePoint, etc.) with access settings. Evidence that all employees can access it.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: Statement that policies are accessible without showing where or how. Link to a repository without access config.
red_flags: Policies stored in personal drives or email only
Access restricted to a small group (not all relevant personnel)
No central repository (policies scattered across systems)

AST-01.title: Information Asset Inventory
AST-01.description: {company_name} maintains an inventory of its information assets, from infrastructure and applications to data stores and endpoints, each with a designated owner. The inventory and documented data flows are reviewed periodically for accuracy.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization maintain an inventory of information assets (systems, data stores, hardware)? (Yes/No, even a spreadsheet counts)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have information asset inventory practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.

evidence_commands.command: aws iam generate-credential-report; aws iam get-credential-report --output text --query Content | base64 -d
evidence_commands.shows: Generates then downloads the IAM credential report (CSV) covering every account: password and access key age, last used date, and MFA status. Look for active accounts with no MFA device attached, or credentials untouched beyond 12 months, which shows the identity/asset inventory isn't being reviewed and pruned. Note: the original single get-credential-report call can fail with a report-in-progress error on first run, so generate-credential-report must run first.

Lists every IAM user with creation date and last console login. An account with an old CreateDate and a blank or very old PasswordLastUsed is the tell of a stale, un-inventoried account that should have been deprovisioned.

Returns account-wide totals for users, groups, roles, and MFA devices enabled. An MFADevices count meaningfully lower than the Users count is the fail signal that the identity inventory includes accounts without MFA.

Returns the Okta MFA enrollment policy, including which factors are required and which groups it applies to. A status of INACTIVE, or a policy that doesn't cover all active user groups, is the fail signal.

evidence_commands.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: SSWS {api_token}' 'https://{domain}.okta.com/api/v1/users?limit=200' | python3 -c "import sys,json; users=json.load(sys.stdin); print(f'Total users: {len(users)}'); [print(f'{u[\"profile\"][\"email\"]}: {u[\"status\"]}') for u in users[:20]]"
evidence_commands.shows: Lists every Okta user account with its status (ACTIVE, STAGED, DEPROVISIONED, and so on). A STAGED or DEPROVISIONED account still listed past the entity's offboarding window, or a user count that doesn't reconcile with current headcount, is the fail signal for an inventory that isn't kept current.

Lists every member of the GitHub organization with their role. An account still listed for someone who has left the company is the fail signal for an asset inventory that isn't reconciled against current headcount.

Lists every Google Workspace account with its suspension state and last sign in date. A non suspended, active account with no recent login is the fail signal that the identity inventory still includes an account that should have been removed.

Lists every 1Password account member and their state (active, suspended, deprovisioned). A member left in an active state after departure is the fail signal that the credential/asset inventory isn't reconciled against offboarding.

collection.question: Do you maintain an inventory of your information assets, infrastructure, applications, data stores, and integrations?
follow_ups: Does each asset have a designated owner?
How often is the inventory reviewed for accuracy?
Do you have data flow diagrams showing how data moves through your systems?

evidence_goals: Pull the current asset inventory itself (spreadsheet, CMDB export, or asset management platform view) covering infrastructure, applications, data stores, endpoints, and external integrations
Pull the owner assignments showing each listed asset has a designated owner
Pull the data flow documentation or architecture diagram showing how data moves between system components and external parties
Pull the inventory review record showing when it was last checked for accuracy, by whom, and what changed
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: A maintained inventory (live view or export) that lists every asset with a named owner and spans all in scope categories, accompanied by a current data flow diagram and a dated review record showing a real person confirmed accuracy within the stated period.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: A one time snapshot with the owner column blank, whole categories missing (no data stores or third party integrations listed), no data flow documentation, and no evidence anyone reviews it.
red_flags: Inventory has no owner column, or owners are left blank
Whole asset categories are absent, such as no data stores or no external integrations
No data flow diagram, or it predates the current architecture
No review record, or the last review is older than the stated frequency
Inventory is a stale export with production systems missing

platform_hints.notion: The asset inventory and data flow documentation often live in a Notion database or page. Pull the full view and check for an owner property and a last reviewed date on entries.
platform_hints.google_workspace: The inventory is commonly a Google Sheet. Pull the sheet and check the owner column is populated and the revision history shows recent maintenance.
platform_hints.aws: Corroborate the listed infrastructure against a live resource list (compute, databases, object storage) to confirm the inventory reflects what is actually running.
platform_hints.github: Corroborate the listed applications and repositories against the actual repository list to catch systems missing from the inventory.

AST-02.title: Data Classification
AST-02.description: {company_name} classifies data by sensitivity, with defined handling, storage, access, and disposal requirements per level, and communicates the scheme to personnel who handle data.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization classify data by sensitivity level (e.g., public, confidential, restricted)? (Yes/No)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have data classification practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.

evidence_commands.shows: Lists every KMS key in the region with its key ID and ARN. A classified or sensitive data store with no corresponding key referenced anywhere, or a key in a disabled or pending-deletion state that's still in use, is the fail signal.
Reports each RDS instance's StorageEncrypted flag and the KMS key used. A production instance holding classified data with StorageEncrypted set to false is the fail signal.

evidence_commands.command: aws s3api list-buckets --query 'Buckets[*].Name' --output text | while read b; do echo "$b: $(aws s3api get-bucket-encryption --bucket $b 2>&1)"; done
evidence_commands.shows: Reports the default encryption configuration for every S3 bucket in the account. A ServerSideEncryptionConfigurationNotFoundError returned for a bucket known to hold classified data is the fail signal.
Lists every EBS volume with its Encrypted flag and KMS key. An unencrypted volume attached to a production instance that handles classified data is the fail signal.

evidence_commands.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer {api_token}' 'https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/zones/{zone_id}/settings' | python3 -c "import sys,json; settings=json.load(sys.stdin)['result']; [print(f'{s[\"id\"]}: {s[\"value\"]}') for s in settings if s['id'] in ['ssl','min_tls_version','always_use_https','waf']]"
evidence_commands.shows: Retrieves the zone's TLS and firewall settings. A min_tls_version below 1.2, ssl not set to strict or full strict, or waf turned off is the fail signal that data in transit isn't protected to the level its classification requires.

Lists every KMS key in the given keyring with its creation date and rotation period. A classified data store on Google Cloud with no corresponding key, or a key with rotation disabled, is the fail signal for entities running on GCP instead of AWS.

Lists every enrolled mobile device with its encryption status. A device reporting unencrypted while its status is active is the fail signal that data classified as sensitive isn't protected on endpoints that access it.

collection.question: Do you classify your data by sensitivity level with defined handling requirements?
follow_ups: What classification levels do you use?
Are handling, storage, and disposal requirements defined for each level?
Is the classification scheme communicated to employees who handle data?

evidence_goals: Pull the data classification scheme showing the defined sensitivity levels
Pull the handling requirements for each level covering storage, access, transmission, and disposal
Pull evidence the scheme is actually applied to real data assets, such as labels on the asset inventory or data catalog, not just defined on paper
Pull the record showing the scheme was communicated to personnel who handle data, such as training completion or policy acknowledgment records
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: A classification policy defining each sensitivity level with concrete handling rules for storage, access, transmission, and disposal, alongside an inventory or data catalog where real assets carry those labels and records showing the people who handle data were trained on the scheme.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: A policy that names classification levels in the abstract with no per level handling rules, no evidence any actual data has been classified, and no proof staff were told the scheme exists.
red_flags: Levels are named but no handling requirements are defined for each
Scheme is defined on paper but no data assets actually carry classification labels
Disposal or transmission requirements are missing from the handling rules
No training or acknowledgment showing staff know the scheme
A label contradicts the asset inventory, such as an asset marked public that holds customer data

platform_hints.notion: The classification policy and the data catalog where labels are applied often live in Notion. Pull both and confirm labels appear on real entries, not only in a template.
platform_hints.google_workspace: Training or acknowledgment evidence is commonly a Google Form or shared doc. Pull the completion records covering the people who handle data.

AST-03.title: SaaS & Data Asset Inventory
AST-03.description: {company_name} maintains an inventory of the SaaS applications and tools it uses, identifying which hold customer or confidential data, reviews the inventory on a defined cadence, and adds new tools as they are adopted.

collection.gating_question: Do you keep a list of the SaaS tools and applications your company uses, including which ones hold customer data? (Yes/No)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have SaaS and data asset inventory practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.
collection.question: How do you track the SaaS applications and tools your company uses and which of them hold customer or sensitive data?
follow_ups: Where is the SaaS or tool inventory kept, and when was it last updated?
Does the inventory note which tools hold customer or confidential data?
How does a newly adopted tool get added to the inventory?

evidence_commands.shows: The third-party applications connected to workspace accounts via OAuth, which can be reconciled against the maintained tool inventory so unlisted SaaS tools surface.
Integrations connected to the code organization, a second source to reconcile against the SaaS inventory so tools missing from the list are identified.

evidence_goals: Obtain the SaaS and tool inventory with an owner and last-updated date
Obtain the data sensitivity noted for each entry, in particular which tools hold customer data
Obtain evidence the inventory is reviewed on a cadence and new tools are added
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: A maintained sheet or database listing each SaaS tool with owner, purpose, and the sensitivity of data it holds, carrying recent review or update dates. The list reconciles with the OAuth and integration connections the core systems report.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: A stale list with no dates, or an inventory that omits tools the identity provider or workspace shows are connected and holding data.
red_flags: No indication of which tools hold customer or confidential data
Inventory not updated in over twelve months
Connected SaaS apps that do not appear in the inventory
No owner assigned to maintain the inventory

platform_hints.google_workspace: Use the token or connected-apps report to list OAuth-connected SaaS and reconcile against the inventory.
platform_hints.github: List organization app installations to find connected tools that touch the codebase.
platform_hints.notion: A Notion database with dated entries and a data-sensitivity property is acceptable evidence of a maintained inventory at this scale.

COM-01.title: Customer Commitments & Service Descriptions
COM-01.description: {company_name} documents its security commitments to customers in contracts, SLAs, privacy policies, or trust pages. Customer responsibilities, system objectives, and how the service operates are communicated to external users.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization describe its services, commitments, and security practices to customers? (Yes/No, even in a terms of service or trust page)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have customer commitments and service descriptions practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.
collection.question: How do you communicate your security commitments and responsibilities to customers?
follow_ups: Do you have SLAs, a trust page, or security documentation available to customers?
Are customer responsibilities (like securing their own credentials) documented?
Do you have a privacy policy published?

evidence_goals: Pull the customer facing commitment documents (a sample contract or master service agreement with security clauses, an SLA, the privacy policy, or the public trust page)
Pull the documented customer responsibilities (shared responsibility model, trust page section, or contract clause listing what the customer must do)
Pull evidence that changes to commitments are communicated to customers, such as a trust page changelog, a notification email, or a contract amendment process
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: Actual customer facing documents, such as a signed contract with security clauses or a published trust page and privacy policy, that state commitments consistent with how the system actually operates, spell out what the customer is responsible for, and show a real mechanism for notifying customers when commitments change.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: A statement that commitments exist without the underlying documents, a trust page that promises controls the system does not actually run, or no documented customer responsibilities at all.
red_flags: Commitments are described but no contract, SLA, privacy policy, or trust page is produced
Public commitments promise controls the entity does not actually operate
No documented split between customer and provider responsibilities
No mechanism for telling customers when commitments change
The privacy policy or trust page is outdated relative to current practice

COM-02.title: External Reporting & Inbound Communication
COM-02.description: External parties can report security issues through accessible, published channels. What comes in is evaluated and routed to the people responsible for acting on it.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization have processes for external reporting (status page, security contact) and handling inbound security communications? (Yes/No)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have external reporting and inbound communication practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.
collection.question: How can external parties report security concerns or issues to you?
follow_ups: Do you have a security@ email or responsible disclosure page?
Do you have a status page for service availability?
How are inbound security reports triaged?

evidence_goals: Pull the external security reporting channel configuration (security.txt, bug bounty, contact page)
Pull the anonymous or confidential reporting mechanism configuration
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: Actual URL or config showing how external parties can report security issues. Config of anonymous reporting channel (ethics hotline, form, email alias).
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: Statement that reporting channels exist without showing them. Policy document without actual channel config.
red_flags: No public way to report security issues
No anonymous or confidential reporting option
Reporting channel not monitored or response not defined

RSK-01.title: Annual Risk Assessment
RSK-01.description: {company_name} performs a formal risk assessment periodically covering: identification of internal and external threats, evaluation of vulnerabilities, estimation of likelihood and impact, and risk response decisions. The assessment includes vendor risks, fraud risks, changes to the business environment, systems, technology, and threats.

collection.gating_question: Has your organization conducted any kind of risk assessment for security or technology risks? (Yes/No, even informal)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have annual risk assessment practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.
collection.question: Do you perform a formal risk assessment, and how often?
follow_ups: What methodology do you use (likelihood/impact matrix, NIST, custom)?
Does it cover fraud risk, vendor risk, and technology change risk?
Who participates in the risk assessment?
How are risk responses documented (accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid)?

evidence_goals: Pull the risk assessment or risk register itself, dated within the stated period
Pull the sections showing risks are identified across the whole entity, including entity level, application, infrastructure, vendor, and fraud risks, with likelihood and impact estimated for each
Pull the risk response decision recorded for each risk (accept, avoid, reduce, or share)
Pull the version history or update log showing the assessment is refreshed when significant business or technology changes occur
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: A dated risk assessment or risk register from within the stated period that identifies internal and external threats across the entity including vendor and fraud risks, estimates likelihood and impact for each risk, records a response decision for every risk, and shows an update history tied to significant changes.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: An undated or years old document, or a generic threat list copied from a template with no likelihood, impact, or response recorded per risk, no vendor or fraud coverage, and no evidence it is ever updated.
red_flags: Risk assessment is undated or older than the stated frequency
Likelihood and impact are not estimated per risk
No risk response is recorded (risks are listed but nothing is decided)
Fraud risk and vendor risk are absent
Generic template with no entity specific risks, or no update history despite major changes in the business

platform_hints.notion: The risk register is often a Notion database. Pull the full export and check the date, plus per row likelihood, impact, and response columns.
platform_hints.google_workspace: The risk assessment is commonly a Google Doc or Sheet. Pull it and use the revision history to confirm it was performed within the stated period and updated after significant changes.

RSK-02.title: Risk-Based Control Design
RSK-02.description: Control activities are selected and designed to address the risks identified in the risk assessment, with a documented mapping showing how each risk is covered, including the IT general controls the business depends on.

collection.gating_question: Are your security controls designed or chosen based on identified risks? (Yes/No)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have risk-based control design practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.
collection.question: How do your security controls map to the risks you've identified?
follow_ups: Is there a documented link between risks and the controls that address them?
How do you determine if a control is sufficient for a given risk?

evidence_goals: Pull the risk to control mapping showing each identified risk is linked to the control that addresses it
Pull evidence that every significant risk has at least one control, with no high or critical risk left unaddressed
Pull the general IT controls documentation covering logical access, system operations, and change management
Pull the documentation showing which business processes depend on which technology controls
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: A mapping that traces each risk from the risk assessment to one or more controls, leaves no significant risk unaddressed, covers the core IT general controls across access, operations, and change management, and names which business processes depend on which technology.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: A control list with no link back to identified risks, significant risks with no matching control, or IT general controls described in the abstract with no connection to the entity's actual systems.
red_flags: No documented link between risks and controls
High or critical risks with no control assigned
Control list exists but is not derived from the risk assessment
IT general controls do not cover all three of access, operations, and change management
No mapping of which business processes depend on technology

platform_hints.notion: The risk to control mapping is often a Notion database or table linked to the risk register. Pull it and confirm each risk row references a control and no significant risk is blank.

IAM-01.title: User Authentication
IAM-01.description: {company_name} requires users to be uniquely identified and authenticated before accessing production systems and business applications. Authentication mechanisms are appropriate for the sensitivity of the systems accessed.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization use a centralized identity provider or authentication system (such as Okta, Google Workspace, Azure AD, Auth0)? (Yes/No)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have user authentication practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.

evidence_commands.command: aws iam get-credential-report --output text --query Content | base64 -d
evidence_commands.shows: A per-user CSV showing password_enabled, mfa_active, and last-used timestamps for every IAM user; look for accounts with password_enabled=true but no corresponding individual owner, or user names suggesting a shared login (admin, devteam, shared).

The full IAM user roster with creation date and last password use; look for generic or shared-sounding usernames, or users with PasswordLastUsed blank despite being long-lived, which would indicate the account isn't tied to an individually authenticated person.

Account-wide totals including Users and AccountAccessKeysPresent; look for AccountAccessKeysPresent=1, which means the shared root account (not an individually identified user) has active programmatic credentials.

The organization's authentication enrollment policy including which factor types are required and which groups it applies to; look for a policy with status INACTIVE or a scope that excludes production-access groups.

evidence_commands.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: SSWS {api_token}' 'https://{domain}.okta.com/api/v1/users?limit=200' | python3 -c "import sys,json; users=json.load(sys.stdin); print(f'Total users: {len(users)}'); [print(f'{u[\"profile\"][\"email\"]}: {u[\"status\"]}') for u in users[:20]]"
evidence_commands.shows: Each directory user's email and status (ACTIVE, SUSPENDED, DEPROVISIONED); look for a shared or generic email address, or a user still marked ACTIVE who should have been suspended, indicating accounts are not uniquely and currently authenticated individuals.

collection.question: How do users authenticate to your production systems and business applications?
follow_ups: Does everyone have unique user IDs (no shared accounts)?
What is your password policy (length, complexity, expiry)?
Which systems use SSO vs local authentication?
documents: Identity Provider (Okta / Azure AD / Google Workspace)

evidence_goals: Pull user list showing unique identifiers per user (no shared accounts)
Pull authentication policy configuration (password policy, session settings)
Pull list of standalone or local accounts not managed through the identity provider
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: User list showing individual accounts (no shared logins). Password policy config with complexity and expiration settings. List of any local/standalone accounts with documented justification.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: Statement that everyone has unique accounts without showing the user list. Password policy document without actual system config.
red_flags: Shared accounts (admin@company.com, ops@, etc.)
No password complexity requirements
Local accounts on production systems without justification
Inactive accounts still enabled

platform_hints.okta: Pull user list with status. Pull password policy config. Pull sign-on policy. Check for shared or generic accounts in user directory.
platform_hints.auth0: Pull user list from Management API. Pull password policy from connection settings. Pull authentication rules.
platform_hints.supabase: Pull auth user list. Check email/password policy settings. Pull any service role or anon key usage.

IAM-02.title: Multi-Factor Authentication
IAM-02.description: Multi-factor authentication is enforced for access to production infrastructure, cloud consoles, code repositories, business-critical applications, and remote connections.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization use multi-factor authentication (MFA) on any of your systems? (Yes/No)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have multi-factor authentication practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.

evidence_commands.command: aws iam get-credential-report --output text --query Content | base64 -d
evidence_commands.shows: The mfa_active column for every IAM user with console access; look for mfa_active=false on any user whose password_enabled is also true, meaning that person can sign in without a second factor.
The population of console-capable IAM users to cross-reference against the credential report's mfa_active flags; look for any user on this list who does not appear with an active MFA device.

Account-wide MFADevices and MFADevicesInUse counts alongside total Users, plus AccountMFAEnabled for the root account; look for MFADevicesInUse lower than Users, or AccountMFAEnabled=0, meaning the root account itself lacks MFA.

The configured MFA enrollment policy, its required factor types, and the group(s) it is scoped to; look for a policy status of INACTIVE or a scope that omits a group with access to production systems.

evidence_commands.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: SSWS {api_token}' 'https://{domain}.okta.com/api/v1/users?limit=200' | python3 -c "import sys,json; users=json.load(sys.stdin); print(f'Total users: {len(users)}'); [print(f'{u[\"profile\"][\"email\"]}: {u[\"status\"]}') for u in users[:20]]"
evidence_commands.shows: The active user population to size the MFA enrollment check against; combine with the enrollment policy output to confirm every ACTIVE user falls under a group that requires MFA, and look for ACTIVE users outside any MFA-required group.
Whether the GitHub organization enforces two-factor authentication for all members; look for a returned value of false, meaning members can access repositories with only a password.
The list of organization members who currently have 2FA disabled; look for any login returned at all, since a fully enforced organization returns an empty list.
Per-user 2-step verification enrollment and enforcement flags in Google Workspace; look for isEnrolledIn2Sv=False on any account, especially ones with admin console access.

collection.question: Is multi-factor authentication required for all users accessing production systems and critical applications?
follow_ups: Which identity provider enforces MFA?
Are any users or service accounts exempt from MFA?
Is MFA enrollment required or optional?
documents: Identity Provider (Okta / Azure AD / Google Workspace)

evidence_goals: Pull the MFA policy configuration for the organization
Pull a user list or report showing MFA enrollment status per user
Pull the list of allowed authentication factors (authenticator app, hardware key, SMS, etc.)
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: Raw policy config or API output showing the enforcement setting (required vs optional) plus a user-level report showing enrollment status per user. Actual settings, not a summary.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: Verbal confirmation that MFA is enabled without config proof. A screenshot. A summary without the enforcement setting or per-user status.
red_flags: MFA set to optional or prompted but not enforced
Service accounts or shared accounts excluded from MFA requirement
Admin or privileged accounts not covered by MFA policy
SMS as the only allowed factor
Large number of users showing not enrolled

platform_hints.okta: Pull Sign-On Policy rules and MFA enrollment policy. Pull per-user MFA enrollment status. Check if any groups are excluded.
platform_hints.auth0: Pull MFA policy from tenant settings. Check per-user MFA enrollment. Check Rules or Actions related to MFA.

IAM-03.title: User Access Provisioning
IAM-03.description: Prior to granting access, the entity registers and authorizes the user and documents the access granted. This applies to all access provisioning including new hires, role changes, contractor onboarding, and temporary access grants.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization have a process for granting access to systems when someone joins or changes roles? (Yes/No)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have user access provisioning practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.

evidence_commands.command: aws iam get-credential-report --output text --query Content | base64 -d
evidence_commands.shows: Each user's CreateDate, which should align with a documented provisioning request; look for a user creation date with no corresponding onboarding ticket or approval record for that time period.

evidence_commands.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: SSWS {api_token}' 'https://{domain}.okta.com/api/v1/users?limit=200' | python3 -c "import sys,json; users=json.load(sys.stdin); print(f'Total users: {len(users)}'); [print(f'{u[\"profile\"][\"email\"]}: {u[\"status\"]}') for u in users[:20]]"
evidence_commands.shows: The current directory population and each user's status; look for an active user with no matching provisioning ticket, or a user provisioned before their documented start date.

Each account's creation timestamp and assigned organizational unit; look for a creation date that predates the documented approval or an org unit that grants broader access than the person's role warrants.

collection.question: How is access granted to new employees or when someone changes roles?
follow_ups: Is there a formal approval process before access is granted?
Are access requests documented (tickets, email approvals)?
Is access role-based or individually assigned?
documents: Identity Provider (Okta / Azure AD / Google Workspace)

evidence_goals: Pull the written provisioning procedure or onboarding checklist that lists the access-granting steps
Pull a sample of provisioning records for recent new hires or role changes, showing the access request and its approval
Pull the current per-user access list from the identity provider to compare against what was authorized
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: The written procedure plus, for named recent joiners or role changes, the actual request-and-approval record (a ticket or an email from an authorized manager or system owner) matched against the access that now appears in the identity provider.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: A procedure document with no completed request or approval records behind it, or a statement that a manager approves access verbally with nothing captured.
red_flags: Approvals missing entirely for sampled access grants
Approver is the same person who received the access, or has no authority to approve it
Access provisioned is broader than what was requested and approved
No records exist for the earliest hires because the process started recently
Standing access granted to new joiners by default without a request

platform_hints.okta: Pull per-user assignments and group memberships to confirm what access was actually granted. Compare against the approval records.
platform_hints.google_workspace: Pull the Admin console user list and group memberships to confirm granted access for sampled joiners.
platform_hints.github: Pull organization membership and team assignments for sampled joiners to confirm repository access matches the approval.
platform_hints.linear: Provisioning approval tickets or issues often live here. Pull the request and the approver comment or state change.
platform_hints.notion: Onboarding checklists and access-request records are often kept here. Pull the completed instance, not the template.

IAM-04.title: User Access Deprovisioning
IAM-04.description: System access is revoked promptly at termination and adjusted on role changes, with offboarding completion tracked so no credential stays valid longer than it should.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization have a process for removing access when someone leaves or changes roles? (Yes/No)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have user access deprovisioning practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.

evidence_commands.command: aws iam get-credential-report --output text --query Content | base64 -d
evidence_commands.shows: Each user's password_enabled and access_key_active flags with last-used dates; look for a terminated employee's account still showing password_enabled=true or an active access key after their termination date.

evidence_commands.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: SSWS {api_token}' 'https://{domain}.okta.com/api/v1/users?limit=200' | python3 -c "import sys,json; users=json.load(sys.stdin); print(f'Total users: {len(users)}'); [print(f'{u[\"profile\"][\"email\"]}: {u[\"status\"]}') for u in users[:20]]"
evidence_commands.shows: Each user's current status; look for a terminated employee whose account still shows ACTIVE rather than SUSPENDED or DEPROVISIONED, and check the status-change timestamp against the termination date.

evidence_commands.command: gam print users query "isSuspended=true" fields primaryEmail,suspended,lastLoginTime
evidence_commands.shows: The list of suspended Google Workspace accounts with their last login time; look for a terminated employee absent from this list entirely, meaning their account was never suspended, or a long gap between the termination date and the suspension action.

Every 1Password account user and their state (active, suspended, or deleted); look for a terminated employee still listed as active, meaning their access to shared credential vaults was never revoked.

collection.question: What happens to a person's access when they leave the company or change roles?
follow_ups: How quickly is access revoked after departure (same day, within 24 hours)?
Is there an automated process or manual checklist?
Does the process cover all systems (cloud, code repos, SaaS tools)?
documents: Identity Provider (Okta / Azure AD / Google Workspace)

evidence_goals: Pull the written offboarding procedure or checklist covering access-revocation steps and the required timeframe
Pull the list of departures during the period from the HR system, with termination dates
Pull identity provider account status showing deactivation dates, to compare timing against the termination dates
Pull evidence of access removal across all in-scope systems for a sample of leavers
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: For named leavers, the HR termination date matched against the identity provider deactivation timestamp inside the policy window, plus confirmation the account was removed from every in-scope system, not just the primary directory.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: A blank checklist template with no completed instances, or a claim that access is removed promptly without any dated deactivation records to prove it.
red_flags: A terminated person still shows as active in the identity provider or a code repository
Deactivation date is well after the termination date, beyond the policy window
Directory account disabled but code repository, database, or SaaS access left in place
No termination dates available to compare removal timing against
Offboarding steps have no timestamps, so timeliness cannot be verified

platform_hints.okta: Pull per-user status and the deactivation date for sampled leavers. Compare against the HR termination date.
platform_hints.google_workspace: Pull the user list showing suspended or deleted status and the date it changed for sampled leavers.
platform_hints.github: Confirm sampled leavers were removed from organization membership and all teams. Check for lingering outside-collaborator access.
platform_hints.gusto: Termination dates for sampled leavers come from here. Pull the record showing the departure date.
platform_hints.rippling: Pull termination dates and, where offboarding is automated, the app-deprovisioning log for sampled leavers.

IAM-05.title: Periodic User Access Reviews
IAM-05.description: System owners or management review user access periodically, verifying access matches current job responsibilities and remediating anything inappropriate promptly.

collection.gating_question: Do you conduct periodic reviews of user access, where someone checks who has access to what and decides if it's still appropriate? (Yes/No, informal reviews count as yes)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have periodic user access reviews practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.

evidence_commands.command: aws iam get-credential-report --output text --query Content | base64 -d
evidence_commands.shows: The full IAM user population with password and key activity to compare against the access review's sign-off list; look for a user present in the account but absent from the review, meaning they were not covered by the last review cycle.

evidence_commands.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: SSWS {api_token}' 'https://{domain}.okta.com/api/v1/users?limit=200' | python3 -c "import sys,json; users=json.load(sys.stdin); print(f'Total users: {len(users)}'); [print(f'{u[\"profile\"][\"email\"]}: {u[\"status\"]}') for u in users[:20]]"
evidence_commands.shows: The current active directory population to reconcile against the reviewer's sign-off list; look for a user missing from the review documentation, or one flagged for removal during the review who still shows ACTIVE here after the remediation deadline.

Each access group's name and member count (via the stats expansion); look for a group with a materially different member count than the last review documented, indicating access changed without a corresponding review update.

Every repository collaborator and their permission level (admin, write, triage, read); look for a collaborator whose role_name exceeds what the access review approved, or a former team member still listed.

Every direct and inherited project member with their access_level; look for a member whose access level was not addressed in the last review, or one whose role has since changed without a corresponding access update.
Current Supabase organization members and their roles; look for a member whose role was not covered by the last access review, or a former team member still listed as a member.
Current members of the deployment team and their access role; look for a member whose role has not been revisited since the documented review date, or a role broader than their job function requires.

collection.question: Do you conduct periodic reviews of user access across your systems?
follow_ups: How often are reviews performed (quarterly, semi-annually)?
Who performs the review?
What happens when inappropriate access is found?
Are review results documented?
documents: Identity Provider (Okta / Azure AD / Google Workspace)

evidence_goals: Pull the policy language that requires access reviews, naming the reviewer role and the frequency
Pull the completed, dated review records produced during the period
Pull the list of in-scope systems, to confirm each review covered all of them
Pull remediation records for any access flagged during a review, showing it was actioned
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: Dated completed review artifacts (a signed-off spreadsheet, a ticket, or an access-certification export) covering every in-scope system at the required cadence, with each reviewer being the system owner or a designated authority, and any revocations traced through to completion.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: A claim that reviews happen with no dated artifact to show for a period, or a single review that covered only the identity provider while the code repository and database were never looked at.
red_flags: No dated review record exists for the period under examination
Review covers the directory only and omits code repositories, databases, or key SaaS tools
Reviewer is not the system owner or a designated authority, or the review has no named reviewer
Reviews scheduled but skipped, so the cadence is not met
Access flagged as inappropriate during a review with no evidence it was removed

platform_hints.okta: If an access-certification or review campaign feature is used, pull the completed campaign export showing reviewer, date, and decisions. Otherwise the review artifact lives outside the tool.
platform_hints.google_workspace: The user and group list is the input to a review. The review itself is the dated record of someone signing off on it, kept separately.
platform_hints.github: Organization membership and team lists are the review input. Pull the dated record confirming these were reviewed and any removals that followed.
platform_hints.notion: Review spreadsheets or sign-off pages are often kept here. Pull the dated completed record, not a blank template.

IAM-06.title: Role-Based Access & Least Privilege
IAM-06.description: Access is granted based on job function using defined roles. Users receive only the minimum access required for their duties.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization use roles or groups to manage access permissions (rather than individual grants)? (Yes/No)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have role-based access and least privilege practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.

evidence_commands.shows: Each defined access group with its member count via the stats expansion; look for a single generic group (like "all employees") granting broad application access rather than role-scoped groups mapped to job function.
Each collaborator's role_name against the repository; look for individual contributors holding admin instead of write or triage, which would exceed the minimum access their job function requires.

Each member's access_level (Guest through Owner) mapped against their defined role; look for a member holding Maintainer or Owner access with no documented business need beyond a standard Developer role.

Role bindings mapping each principal (user, group, or service account) to the IAM roles granted on the project; look for broad predefined roles like roles/owner or roles/editor granted directly to individuals instead of scoped roles matching their job function.

collection.question: How do you implement least privilege and role-based access in your systems?
follow_ups: Are roles defined with specific permissions for each system?
How do you ensure users only have the access they need?
Are role assignments reviewed regularly?
documents: Identity Provider (Okta / Azure AD / Google Workspace)

evidence_goals: Pull the list of defined access roles or groups with their associated permissions
Pull user-to-role or user-to-group assignments showing access is role-based
Pull any individual permission grants (not through roles)
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: Role or group list with permission descriptions. User assignments showing access through roles, not individual grants. Config showing role-based access is the standard mechanism.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: Statement that RBAC is used without showing roles or assignments. Org chart instead of access config.
red_flags: Permissions granted directly to users (not through roles)
Roles with overly broad permissions (full admin for non-admin functions)
No documentation of what each role can access
Single role assigned to all users (no differentiation)

platform_hints.okta: Pull groups with member counts. Pull application assignments (group-based vs individual). Pull admin role assignments.

IAM-07.title: Privileged Access Management
IAM-07.description: Privileged access is limited to personnel with a documented business need. Privileged and service accounts are inventoried with named owners, and privileged activity is logged.

collection.gating_question: Does your organization manage privileged or administrative access separately from regular access? (Yes/No)
collection.absent_reason_template: Entity does not have privileged access management practices in place. All attributes for this control marked absent. This is a structural gap requiring implementation.

evidence_commands.shows: Privileged/admin access groups and their member counts via the stats expansion; look for a group name indicating elevated access (admin, superuser) with more members than the documented list of authorized privileged users.
Everyone holding the admin role_name on the repository; look for an admin who is not on the entity's documented list of authorized privileged users.
Members with Owner or Maintainer access_level; look for a privileged member without a documented business justification, or a privileged role never inventoried by the entity.

evidence_commands.command: aws iam get-credential-report --output text --query Content | base64 -d
evidence_commands.shows: Every IAM user's activity, cross-referenced against the entity's privileged-user list; look for a user with administrator-level permissions who is not on the documented privileged access inventory.

The full IAM user population to reconcile against the privileged access inventory; look for a user with an administrator-level attached policy whose name does not appear on the entity's documented list of privileged personnel.
The specific principals holding owner or editor (privileged) roles on the project; look for more principals here than appear on the entity's documented privileged access inventory.

The shared vaults in use, to pair with a per-vault group/user access check; look for a vault holding production secrets that is shared with a broad group rather than the specific individuals with a documented business need.

collection.question: How is privileged or admin access managed and monitored?
follow_ups: Are admin accounts separate from regular user accounts?
How many people have admin access to production?
Is privileged access activity logged and reviewed?
documents: Identity Provider (Okta / Azure AD / Google Workspace)

evidence_goals: Pull the list of privileged or admin users across in-scope systems
Pull authorization records or justification for each privileged account
Pull audit logging configuration for privileged actions
collection_playbook.what_good_looks_like: Per-system list of admin or privileged accounts. Documentation of why each account has elevated access. Config showing privileged actions are logged.
collection_playbook.what_bad_looks_like: Statement that privileged access is managed without showing who has it. Summary count without per-user detail.
red_flags: Large number of admin accounts relative to team size
Privileged accounts without documented justification
Shared admin accounts
No audit logging for privileged actions
Former employees still in admin lists

platform_hints.okta: Pull admin role assignments. Pull system log config for admin actions. Check super admin count.
platform_hints.github: Pull organization owners and admin list. Pull audit log settings. Check outside collaborators with write access.
